RagShortTexts: Edible woodland fungi can be dried; identification, weather and damp affect supplies.
Dried fungi add to soups while gathering competes with farming, fuel and grain work.

Variants.Content:
Woodland households use familiar edible fungi as seasonal food, recognising them through experience and rejecting decayed portions. Rain, place and season govern the harvest, so no fixed yearly amount can be promised. Distant gathering delays the return, children need watching, and fields, animals and the hearth still require care.

Cutting or spreading fungi for drying reduces weight and helps storage. Strings need ventilation and protection from smoke, dirt and returning damp. Cooks take some for a pot while protecting the remainder from spoilage. Dried fungi add flavour rather than replace grain; market exchanges for salt depend on dryness, cleanliness and transport.
Estate shares should distinguish fresh and dry produce rather than equate their weights. Leaking stores can spoil food already counted as received.
Roadside gathering needs someone who really recognises the food; hunger supplies no identification skill. Dry fungi still need water, pots and fuel and do not replace staple rations.
Drying takes room in a house or shelter. Keeping food or trading for salt depends on grain and weather, while gatherers may share knowledge but guard productive places.
